Stage 3 · Language

Telling people where you are

A short talk is easy to follow when the speaker keeps saying where they are in it.

Read these four lines from a talk.
  • I’m here to talk to you about the meeting nobody needed.
  • First of all, I want to tell you how much time we lose.
  • Let’s move on to why it happens.
  • To sum up: we lose about seven hours a week each.
What do all four have in common?
A listener cannot go back and re-read. Signposts do the job that paragraphs do in writing.

When you read an article, the paragraphing tells you where one idea ends and the next begins. A listener has none of that. Everything they know about the shape of your talk has to come from the words you say, which is why English has a fixed set of signposting phrases and why a talk without them is hard to follow even when every sentence is clear.

There are four signposting jobs. Framing at the start: announcing the topic and, crucially, previewing how many parts there will be (First I want to… Then I’ll… And finally…). Marking each new point as it arrives (The first thing I’d like to mention is… Another factor is…). Transitioning between sections (Now, let’s move on to…). And closing, which in English is a fixed pair of moves: a summary and then an invitation for questions.

The other half of the lesson runs in the opposite direction. Note-taking is the reduction of continuous speech to key words. It works because speech is far more redundant than writing: a two-minute point usually survives as five or six words. The technique is to record content words only — nouns, main verbs, numbers — and drop articles, auxiliaries and prepositions, using indentation to show which detail belongs under which main point.

One category must be recorded exactly rather than paraphrased: numbers, names and dates. Everything else can be compressed; these cannot be reconstructed later if you get them wrong.

Before you look at the table: the tables below give the signposting phrases in the order you use them, followed by the standard note-taking symbols. Read the phrases as a sequence from opening to closing.

CloseTo sum up… · I’d like to finish with… · Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?Tells the audience it is over — they should not have to guess.
Notes, not sentences
What you hearWhat you write

Announce three points and give three. An audience counts. If you say “three things” and give five, people stop following at the fourth.

Signposts carry no content, and that is the job. Let’s move on to tells the listener to close one drawer and open another. Take them out and the same talk becomes much harder to follow.

Write the numbers down first. When you take notes, a number is the one thing you cannot reconstruct afterwards from memory. Everything else you can.

End with the two fixed lines. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions? An audience needs to be told the talk is finished, or the silence does it badly for you.

Full grammar reference — taking notes, and structuring a short talk

What it is

Two connected skills. Note-taking is the systematic reduction of continuous speech to key words, symbols and abbreviations. Talk structure is the reverse operation: expanding a set of notes back into connected speech using signposting language — the phrases that tell an audience where they are.

What it means, and what it does

A talk without signposts leaves listeners guessing when one point ends and the next begins; they cannot go back and re-read. The phrases First of all… Let’s move on to… To sum up… do the job that paragraphs do in writing. Notes, meanwhile, work because speech is far more redundant than writing: a two-minute point usually reduces to five or six words without losing anything.

When and why we use it

When you read an article, the paragraphing tells you where one idea ends and the next begins. A listener has none of that. Everything they know about the shape of your talk has to come from the words you say, which is why English has a fixed set of signposting phrases and why a talk without them is hard to follow even when every sentence is clear.

There are four signposting jobs. Framing at the start: announcing the topic and, crucially, previewing how many parts there will be (First I want to… Then I’ll… And finally…). Marking each new point as it arrives (The first thing I’d like to mention is… Another factor is…). Transitioning between sections (Now, let’s move on to…). And closing, which in English is a fixed pair of moves: a summary and then an invitation for questions.

The other half of the lesson runs in the opposite direction. Note-taking is the reduction of continuous speech to key words. It works because speech is far more redundant than writing: a two-minute point usually survives as five or six words. The technique is to record content words only — nouns, main verbs, numbers — and drop articles, auxiliaries and prepositions, using indentation to show which detail belongs under which main point.

One category must be recorded exactly rather than paraphrased: numbers, names and dates. Everything else can be compressed; these cannot be reconstructed later if you get them wrong.

Typical situations

You need this for giving a presentation at work or in class, explaining something to a group, and taking usable notes in a lecture, a meeting or a training session.

  • Announcing the topic — the opening move that frames everything after it.I’m here to talk to you about something we all do seventy times a day.
  • Previewing the structure — tells the audience how many parts there are.First I want to… Then I’ll… And finally I’ll…
  • Starting the first point — the signal that the preview is over.So, first of all, what factors affect our decision-making?
  • Adding a point — numbering keeps listeners with you.Another major factor is how much information we have.
  • Moving between sections — the clearest of all signposts.Now, let’s move on to how to make a decision.
  • Giving an example — evidence attached to a claim.For example, Charles Darwin is said to have used this method.
  • Summarising — restating the shape before you stop.So, we’ve looked at what affects us and some ways to decide.
  • Closing and inviting questions — the fixed pair of final moves.Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

How it differs from similar structures

Finally = the last point · To sum up = a restatement of all points · In conclusion = written register, heavier in a spoken talk. In a two-minute talk, use To sum up.
Notes = key words for you to speak from · a script = full sentences to read out. Reading a script aloud destroys eye contact; a talk should be given from notes.

How to build it

Open: I’m here to talk to you about + noun phrase
Preview: First, I want to… Then I’ll… And finally, I’ll…
Move on: Let’s move on to + noun / verb-ing
Close: To sum up, + summary sentence → Thank you for listening. → Are there any questions?
OpeningHello, everyone. My name is… and I’m here to talk to you about…
PreviewingIn today’s talk I’m going to look at… First… Then… And finally…
First pointSo, the first thing I’d like to mention is…
AddingAnother factor is… · The third and last point I want to make is…
TransitionNow, let’s move on to… · That brings me to…
ExemplifyingFor example,… · Research seems to show that…
SummarisingSo, we’ve looked at… · To sum up,…
ClosingThank you for listening. Are there any questions?
Note-taking — symbols→ leads to · ↑ increase · ↓ decrease · = is / equals · ≠ is not · + and · & and · # number · ? unclear
Note-taking — abbreviationsinfo, decis., prob. (problem), e.g., i.e., etc., w/ (with), b/c (because), esp. (especially)

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Notes should record content words only — nouns, main verbs, numbers — and drop articles, auxiliaries and prepositions. Making conscious decisions actually makes the brain feel tired becomes more decis. → brain tired.
  • Use indentation to show hierarchy: main point on the left, supporting detail indented under it. This is what makes notes usable later.
  • Numbers, names and dates should be written exactly. Everything else can be paraphrased; these cannot.
  • Let’s move on to is followed by a noun or an -ing form, never a bare infinitive: move on to looking at…
  • To sum up restates; it does not add. Any new information in the summary belongs in the body of the talk.
  • Keep one signpost per transition. Stacking them (So, right, now then, let’s move on…) sounds unprepared.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I’m here for talk to you about decisions. → I’m here to talk to you about decisions.The formula takes the infinitive with to.
  • Let’s move on to look at methods. → Let’s move on to looking at methods.Move on to takes a noun or -ing.
  • To sum up, another factor is stress. → Another factor is stress. … To sum up, three things affect our decisions.A summary restates; it does not introduce a new point.
  • Thanks for your listening. → Thank you for listening.The fixed phrase takes no possessive.
  • Are there some questions? → Are there any questions?Any in questions of this kind.
  • In the end, thank you for listening. → Finally, thank you for listening.In the end reports an outcome, not the last part of a talk.

More examples in context

  • openingHello, everyone. I’m here to talk to you about how we make decisions.
  • previewFirst, I want to look at what affects our decisions. Then I’ll talk about methods. And finally, I’ll give you some tips.
  • first pointSo, the first thing I’d like to mention is the sheer number of decisions we make.
  • evidenceResearch seems to show that making conscious decisions tires the brain.
  • addingAnother major factor is how much information we have to consider.
  • last pointThe third and last factor I want to mention is stress.
  • transitionNow, let’s move on to looking at how to make a decision.
  • exampleFor example, Darwin is said to have made two lists before proposing.
  • summarisingSo, we’ve looked at what affects us, and at two practical methods.
  • closingTo sum up, fewer decisions and less information usually mean better ones. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

A tip for remembering it

Build a talk backwards from its notes. Write your three points as three lines of five words each; that is your whole talk. Then attach a signpost to the front of each line — First of all… Another factor is… The third and last thing… — and add the opening and closing formulas. You will never lose your place, because the signposts tell you and the audience where you are at the same time.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Open by announcing the topic, then preview how many parts there are.
  2. Signpost every transition: First of all… Another… Now let’s move on to…
  3. Move on to is followed by a noun or an -ing form.
  4. Attach an example or evidence to each point.
  5. Summarise with To sum up — restating only, never adding.
  6. Close with Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?
  7. Take notes in content words with indentation; copy numbers and names exactly.

Stage 5 · Main input

A talk that takes three minutes

A few words about meetings

Good morning, everyone. My name is Aigerim Serikova, and I’m here to talk to you about something that costs this company more than almost anything else: the meeting nobody needed.

In today’s talk I’m going to look at three things. First of all, I want to tell you how much time we actually lose. Then I’ll talk about why the meetings get scheduled anyway. And finally, I’ll give you two rules that fixed it for our team.

So, how much time do we lose? We counted for six weeks. The average person in this office sat in eleven hours of meetings a week, and rated four of those hours as useful. That is seven hours a week, or nearly two months a year, per person.

Now, let’s move on to why it happens. In almost every case the meeting was scheduled because somebody was afraid of leaving somebody out — not because there was a decision to make. Politeness, in other words, rather than necessity.

To sum up: we lose about seven hours a week each, and we lose it out of politeness. If you take away two rules today, take these. No meeting without a decision to make, and no meeting without a name next to that decision.

Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

What the model does, in five moves
  • Names the subject in the first sentence, before any warm-up.
  • Announces three points and gives three. Not two, not five.
  • Puts one number in the audience’s head — seven hours — and repeats it at the end.
  • Signposts every change of section, so nobody has to work out where they are.
  • Ends with two fixed lines, so the audience knows to clap.
